overview: This file documents U.S. and international responses to the flow of arms, ammunition, aircraft, fuel, metals, chemicals, machinery, and military technology to Japan and China during and after the Manchurian and Shanghai crises. Its correspondence, legal memoranda, diplomatic reporting, trade statistics, press extracts, and commercial inquiries reveal the State Department’s repeated conclusion that the executive branch lacked authority to embargo private exports without congressional action, as well as concern that an ostensibly neutral embargo on both combatants would disproportionately weaken China. The later papers follow the case-by-case review of proposed American sales and manufacturing licenses to Japanese firms, distinguishing protected military secrets from exportable civilian or previously released technology. The file concludes with translations of Japan’s comprehensive firearms-and-explosives statute and enforcement ordinance, covering manufacture, commerce, possession, storage, transport, inspection, and penalties.
interest: The file is especially valuable for showing how legal limits, commercial interests, military secrecy, and diplomatic strategy interacted before the United States adopted stronger export controls. Its detailed business cases—from aircraft engines and submachine guns to helium, scrap metal, and cartridge-priming machinery—expose the practical boundaries of American neutrality and the incremental transfer of industrial capacity to Japan. Chinese criticism of nondiscriminatory embargoes also illuminates the unequal consequences of formally impartial policies. The translated Japanese law and enforcement ordinance provide an unusually detailed primary source on Japan’s domestic regulation of weapons and explosives.
